components.name: switch
components.title: Switch
components.purpose: An on-or-off setting that takes effect as soon as it changes.
whenToUse: For a setting the app saves the moment it changes, such as Notify me when a run needs approval.
In a list of settings, one switch per row, each with its own label.
whenNotToUse: In a form that is sent with a button. Use a checkbox, which is read as part of the form.
To choose between two named options, such as Unified and Split. Use a segmented control.
To start or stop something that takes time or cannot be undone, such as cancelling a run. Use a button.
To show or hide part of the view from a toolbar. Use an icon button with aria-pressed.
accessibility: Use input type="checkbox" with role="switch" and gw-switch__input, and a label with gw-switch__label whose for attribute is the input's id. A screen reader announces the label, the switch role and on or off.
Inside the div with gw-switch the order is: the label, the state text, the input, then the description and the error if there are any.

The state text is a span with gw-switch__state and aria-hidden="true", holding two spans: gw-switch__on with the word On and gw-switch__off with the word Off. The stylesheet shows the one that matches the input, so no script changes the text. It is hidden from assistive technology because the switch role already says on or off. Always include it: with the thumb's position, it is what keeps the state from resting on colour.
The label names the setting and does not change with the state. Write it so that On means the thing in the label happens.
A description is a p with gw-switch__description, linked from the input with aria-describedby.

The component needs no script to move. The app listens for the change event and saves the setting. If saving fails, it sets the checked property back and adds a p with gw-switch__error and role="alert", linked through aria-describedby, saying which state the setting is in and what to do.
Set the disabled attribute when the setting cannot be changed, and say why in the description.
Tab reaches the switch and Space toggles it. The track is drawn 44px by 24px and its pointer target is 44px each way; a press on the label toggles it too.

components.title: Tab bar
components.purpose: The two to five main destinations of an app, along the bottom of a phone screen, each with an icon and a text label.
whenToUse: For moving between the top-level screens of an app on a phone.
When the app has two to five such screens and every one of them exists.
As the last element in the page, so it sits at the bottom of the screen.
whenNotToUse: At 768px and wider. The bar is not shown there, so list the same destinations in the sidebar nav.
For more than five destinations. Keep the five most used and put the rest behind a menu action in the app header.
For switching between panels inside one view. Use tabs.
For an action such as New task. A destination is a screen, so use a button in the view.

Every link has a text label of one or two words. The icon is decoration and carries aria-hidden="true".
Tab moves through the destinations in order and Enter follows one. Both come from the link element.
The current destination is marked by a bar and a heavier label as well as by colour.
Keep the destinations in the same order on every screen.
The bar is sticky to the bottom of the page. Give the scrolling container scroll-padding-bottom of the bar's height, so a focused element is not hidden under it.

components.name: tabs
components.title: Tabs
components.purpose: A row of tabs that switches between panels of one view, showing one panel at a time.
whenToUse: For two to seven panels that belong to one thing, such as the summary, diff and log of a run, when the reader looks at one at a time.
Wrapped in the gw-tabs element from behaviors/groundwork.js, which handles selection and the arrow keys.
On a plain div with the same classes when the app, such as a React app, sets aria-selected, tabindex and hidden itself.
whenNotToUse: For moving between screens. Use the tab bar below 768px and the sidebar nav at 768px and up, with links and aria-current.
For sections the reader may want open together or scan in one pass. Use an accordion or plain headings.
For a choice that changes a setting or filters a list. Use a select.
For one panel. Show the content with no tabs.

sizes.name: default
sizes.use: Each tab is 44px tall and as wide as its label, at least 44px. A row wider than its container scrolls sideways inside itself, at any width.

accessibility: Markup: a gw-tabs element (or a div) with the gw-tabs class holds one gw-tabs__list with role="tablist" and an aria-label, then one gw-tabs__panel per tab.

Each tab is a button with type="button", role="tab", an id, and aria-controls naming its panel. Each panel has role="tabpanel", an id, aria-labelledby naming its tab, and tabindex="0" so a panel of plain text can take focus.

Write the first state in the markup: aria-selected="true" on one tab and "false" on the rest, and the hidden attribute on every panel but the selected one. The page is then right before any script runs.

What gw-tabs does: on connection and on every selection it sets aria-selected on each tab, tabindex="0" on the selected tab and "-1" on the others, and hidden on every panel except the one the selected tab controls. A click selects a tab. It sets no class and no inline style.

Keyboard, with gw-tabs: Tab moves into the row onto the selected tab, and Tab again moves to the panel. Left and Right move to the previous and next tab and select it, wrapping at the ends. Home selects the first tab and End the last.
Without gw-tabs the app does the same: it sets those three attributes and handles click, Left, Right, Home and End. Nothing else is needed for the styles.
The selected tab is marked by a bar and a heavier label as well as by colour. Never mark it with a class.
Load behaviors/groundwork.js once as a module: <script type="module" src="behaviors/groundwork.js"></script>. Loading it twice is harmless.
While a panel is fetched, set aria-busy="true" on it and show a spinner with text. When the fetch fails, put an alert in the panel that says what to do.
Keep labels to one or two words. A label is never cut: the row scrolls instead, and a tab that takes focus is scrolled into view.

components.name: tag
components.title: Tag
components.purpose: A small neutral label for a category or a filter value, with an optional remove button.
whenToUse: For the categories an item belongs to: labels on a task, the language of a repository.
For each filter applied to a list or a table, with a remove button, in a row above it.
Several at once, in a gw-cluster. Tags are scanned, and no one of them is more important than the next.
whenNotToUse: For a status, such as Failed or Awaiting decision. Use a badge, which has tones and icons. A tag is neutral only.
For something the reader presses to go somewhere or to switch a filter on. Use a link or a button.
For a fact that is not a category, such as a count or a time. Write it as plain text.
For a count on an icon or a tab. Write the count as text.

variants.name: default
variants.use: Text only, on a span, or on an li when the tags are a list.

variants.name: removable
variants.use: The same tag with a button of the class gw-tag__remove after the text. No modifier class is needed.

sizes.name: default
sizes.use: 24px tall with 12px text. A removable tag keeps 8px clear above and below it, so its button's pointer target has room when tags wrap.

accessibility: Use a span. When the tags are a set, such as the filters in force, use a ul with an aria-label that says what they are and an li with the class gw-tag for each.
Write a filter as its name and its value, such as Branch: main, so the tag makes sense out of context.

The remove button is a button element with the class gw-tag__remove and no content. The stylesheet draws its cross. Its aria-label says what it removes and repeats the tag's text: Remove filter: Branch: main.
The button is drawn 22px square, inside the tag's border, and its pointer target is 44px square. Lay removable tags out with gw-cluster so the targets of neighbouring buttons do not overlap.

Tab reaches each remove button in order, and Enter and Space activate it. After a tag is removed, the app moves focus to the next tag's button, or to the control that adds filters when none is left, and says what changed in a role="status" element.
Set the disabled attribute on the button while its filter cannot be removed. A tag with no button at all cannot be removed.
A tag has one tone and never carries meaning by colour.

components.name: tag-input
components.title: Tag input
components.purpose: A box holding the values already added, as removable tags, and a text input for adding the next one.
whenToUse: For several short values of the same kind that the reader types: labels on a task, reviewers, paths an agent may change.
When the values are free text, or come from a list too long to show as checkboxes.
whenNotToUse: For one value. Use a field, or a combobox when it comes from a list.
For a few known options. Use checkboxes.
To show the filters in force on a list. Use tags in a row above the list, with no input.
For long values, such as sentences. Use a textarea, one value to a line.

sizes.name: default
sizes.use: As wide as the field and 54px tall with one row. The box grows as tags wrap.

accessibility: Inside gw-field, after the label, put a div with gw-tag-input. It holds a ul with gw-tag-input__tags and an aria-label that says what the values are, such as Labels added, then an input type="text" with gw-tag-input__input. The label's for attribute matches the input's id.

Each value is an li with the class gw-tag holding its text and a button with gw-tag__remove, copied from the tag component. The button's aria-label names the value: Remove label: backend. Keep the ul in the markup when it is empty.
Say which key adds a value in a gw-field__description linked with aria-describedby: Enter always, and a comma only where a value cannot hold one. On a phone, enterkeyhint="done" labels the key.

The app wires the keys: on Enter or the separator it trims what was typed, appends an li, empties the input and prevents the form from being sent. A pasted list is split on the separator. Backspace in the empty input removes the last tag. Typing the same value twice adds nothing.

After a value is added or removed, say so in a gw-visually-hidden element with role="status", such as backend added, 3 labels. After a remove button is pressed, move focus to the next tag's button, or to the input when none is left.

For a value that cannot be added, leave it in the input, set aria-invalid="true" on the input and link a gw-field__error that repeats the value and says what to type. The box's border turns to the danger colour and the error's icon marks it as well.
Send the values with the form as one hidden input per value, or as the app's own state. The text input holds only the value being typed.
Tab reaches each remove button and then the input. Set disabled on the input and on every remove button when the values cannot change.

whenNotToUse: For one line of text, such as a name or a branch. Use a text input in a field.

components.name: timeline
components.title: Timeline
components.purpose: Events in the order they happened, each with its time, who acted and what happened, joined by a rail.
whenToUse: For the history of one run, task or approval: who did what, and when.
For a run in progress, with the step it is on now marked as the current one.
With the dense variant for a long log of short events.
whenNotToUse: For the messages of a conversation with an agent. Use message rows in a transcript.
For steps the reader has yet to take, such as a setup wizard. This component records what happened.
For a set of things in no particular order. Use the list.
For events compared across columns, or filtered and sorted. Use the data table.
When there are no events, while the first fetch runs or after it fails. Put an empty state, a spinner or an error state in place of the list. Never render an ol with no items.

variants.name: default
variants.use: Time and actor on one line, what happened on the next, 16px between events.

variants.name: dense
variants.use: 8px between events, with what happened on the same line as the time and actor where there is room.

accessibility: Use an ol with one li, gw-timeline__item, for each event, oldest first unless the view says otherwise. A screen reader announces the count and the position.

Each item holds a p with the class gw-timeline__meta and then a p with the class gw-timeline__event. The meta line holds a time element, gw-timeline__time, with a datetime attribute, and the actor, gw-timeline__actor, in words. The event line says what happened as a sentence fragment that starts with a verb.
Write the time so it cannot be misread: the clock time for events of one day, the date as well when the list spans days.

Mark the current step with aria-current="step" on its li and with words in a span of the class gw-timeline__current at the end of the meta line, such as Current step. The filled mark only supports the words.
The rail and the marks are drawn by the stylesheet and are decoration. Nothing is said by them alone.

A long timeline pairs with show-more: render the most recent events, twenty or so, and put one secondary button after the list whose label gives the count, such as Show 34 earlier events. On press the app adds the items to the same ol and moves focus to the first one added. The button is outside the ol.
When an event is added while the reader watches, announce it from a role="status" element in the view, not from the list.
The timeline has no controls of its own and needs no script.

components.purpose: A brief status message that appears at the edge of the screen without taking focus and leaves by itself.
whenToUse: To confirm that something the reader just did has happened, such as a copy or a push.
To report a passing event from elsewhere in the app, such as a run that started, with at most one action.
whenNotToUse: For an action the reader may want to take back. Use the undo toast.
For a failure the reader must act on, or a result that should stay on screen. Use an alert in the view.
For a mistake in a form control. Use the field's error.
For a state of the whole app, such as a lost connection. Use a banner.
For a question. Use a dialog.

variants.name: info
variants.use: The default, with no modifier class. A passing event. The label reads Note.

variants.name: success
variants.use: Something the reader asked for has happened. The label reads Done.

variants.name: danger
variants.use: Something failed and the reader loses nothing by missing the message, or can try again with its one action. The label reads Error.

accessibility: Put one region in the page from the start, as the last element in the body, empty: a div with the class gw-toast__region, role="status", aria-live="polite" and aria-atomic="false". A screen reader announces only what is added to a live region that already exists.

The app shows a toast by appending a gw-toast element to the region and hides it by removing that element. Append the newest last. The stylesheet shows the last three and hides any before them, so remove the oldest when a fourth arrives.
A toast never takes focus. It is announced when the reader's screen reader is next idle.

Each message starts with gw-toast__label holding the tone in words: Note, Done or Error, then a colon. The tone's icon is drawn by the stylesheet. The message is one sentence, and an error says what to do.
A toast has at most one action, a button with gw-button gw-button--small gw-toast__action after the message. Nothing may be reachable only from a toast: the same action is somewhere in the view.

How long it stays is the app's timer: remove a toast without an action after 5 seconds, and one with an action after 10 seconds. Pause the timer while the pointer is over the toast or focus is inside it, and while the page is hidden. Do not remove a danger toast on a timer shorter than 10 seconds.

The region is fixed to the bottom of the screen on a phone and to the bottom trailing corner at 768px and wider, above the page and below nothing but a modal dialog. While a modal dialog is open the page behind it is inert, so report the result of a dialog's action after it closes.

components.name: toggle-button
components.title: Toggle button
components.purpose: A button that turns one view option on or off, such as Wrap lines, and says which with aria-pressed.
whenToUse: For an option of the current view that takes effect at once and is not saved as a setting: Wrap lines, Show whitespace, Show tool calls.
In a toolbar above a log, a diff or a transcript, in its small size.
whenNotToUse: For a setting that is stored, in a settings form. Use a switch, or a checkbox when it is sent with the form.
To choose one of several views, such as Unified or Split. Use a segmented control.
For an option with only an icon. Use an icon button with aria-pressed.
For an action that happens once, such as Copy. Use a button.

variants.name: off
variants.use: aria-pressed="false". Drawn as a plain button.

variants.name: on
variants.use: aria-pressed="true". A stronger border, a sunken fill and a bar under the label.

sizes.name: default
sizes.use: 44px tall.

sizes.name: small
sizes.use: The button component's small size: drawn 32px tall for a toolbar, with a 44px pointer target. Lay small toggles out with gw-cluster gw-gap-md, so the targets of two wrapped rows do not overlap.

accessibility: Use a button element with type="button", the classes gw-button and gw-toggle-button, and aria-pressed set to "true" or "false". The attribute is always present, so a screen reader announces a toggle button in both states.
The label names the option and stays the same in both states: Wrap lines, never Unwrap lines. Only aria-pressed changes. An icon is decoration and carries aria-hidden="true".
The app flips aria-pressed on each press and applies the option at once. Nothing else is needed: the styles read aria-pressed only.
Never add gw-button--primary to show that an option is on.
Group related toggles in an element with role="group" and an aria-label that says what they change, such as Diff view options.
Tab reaches each toggle, and Enter and Space flip it. Both come from the button element.
Set the disabled attribute while the option cannot change. The bar stays, so the reader can still see which options were on.
A toggle button is never busy: the bar is drawn where the button component draws its spinner.

components.name: tool-call
components.title: Tool call
components.purpose: A summary of one tool call outside a transcript: the tool, its target, how it ended and how long it took, with the arguments and output behind disclosures.
whenToUse: In an activity view or a run's detail view, to show one tool call on its own or a short list of them.
When the reader needs the outcome of a call first and its arguments and output only on request.
whenNotToUse: For a tool call as a row of a transcript. Use a message of the tool-call kind, with a tool-result message after it.
For a call that still waits for the reader's answer. Use an approval, which carries Allow and Decline.
For a one-line record of what an agent did, among other events. Use an activity feed entry.

variants.name: succeeded
variants.use: The call returned without an error. The status reads Succeeded beside a check icon.

variants.name: failed
variants.use: The call ran and returned an error. The status reads Failed beside an alert icon, and gw-tool-call__note says what failed.

variants.name: denied
variants.use: The call was refused by the reader or by a permission rule and did not run. The status reads Denied beside a ban icon, and gw-tool-call__note says what was not run and why.

accessibility: Use an article with aria-labelledby pointing at gw-tool-call__title, a heading at the level the view needs. The title holds the tool name and then the target, both as text.
Several calls are li elements of a ul or ol, one article in each.
gw-tool-call__status always holds the status as a word: Running, Succeeded, Failed or Denied. The stylesheet draws the icon from the variant class, so the status is never colour alone.

While the call runs, set aria-busy="true" on the article and leave the variant class off. When it ends, remove aria-busy, add the variant class and change the word. Announce the change from a role="status" element in the view when the reader is waiting on it.
Write the duration with its unit, such as 2.4 s or 48 s so far. A duration that ticks is not in a live region.

Arguments and output each go in a native details element whose summary says what is inside and how long it is, such as Output, 6 lines. They start closed. Enter and Space open and close a summary, and its pointer target is 44px tall.
Write arguments and output as text, never as markup, and write out characters that cannot be seen. gw-tool-call__code wraps and never scrolls sideways.
It holds no action. The component needs no script: the app sets aria-busy, the variant class and the text.

components.name: toolbar
components.title: Toolbar
components.purpose: A row of related controls for one view, grouped and labelled, that wraps or scrolls on a narrow screen.
whenToUse: For three or more controls that act on the same view or selection, such as moving through a diff and showing or hiding its panels.
For toggles and familiar icon actions that should stay one press away while the reader works.
whenNotToUse: For one or two buttons. Put them in a gw-cluster.
For the main action of a view. Show it as the primary button, outside the toolbar.
For a choice between views of the same content. Use a segmented control or tabs.
For the destinations of the app. Use the app header or the sidebar nav.
For fields of a form. A toolbar holds buttons, toggles and a menu button, not text inputs.

variants.name: wrap
variants.use: The default, with no modifier class. Groups that do not fit move to a second row.

variants.name: scroll
variants.use: One row that scrolls sideways inside the toolbar, where a second row would push the content down. Put the controls used most first.

sizes.name: default
sizes.use: Each control is 44px tall, and an icon button 44px square. The toolbar is as wide as its controls and never wider than its container.

accessibility: Use a div with the class gw-toolbar, role="toolbar" and an aria-label that says what the controls act on. Give each toolbar on a page a different label.

The controls are buttons from the button and icon button components, quiet in emphasis: gw-button gw-button--quiet, with gw-icon-button for an icon alone. Every icon button has a name in aria-label or in gw-visually-hidden text.
A toggle carries aria-pressed, "true" or "false", which the app switches on each press. Its name stays the same in both states.

Related controls sit in a div with gw-toolbar__group, role="group" and an aria-label. Between groups goes a div with gw-toolbar__separator, role="separator" and aria-orientation="vertical". A short fact, such as Change 3 of 12, goes in a span with gw-toolbar__text.

For a narrow screen, wrap the least used controls, with their separator, in a div with gw-toolbar__overflow, and add a div with gw-toolbar__more holding an icon button named More actions and a menu with the same actions as items. Below 768px the overflow controls are not rendered and the More button is. At 768px and up it is the other way round.
With no script every control is a tab stop, and Enter and Space activate it. That is complete, if slower than the toolbar pattern.

The roving tabindex is the app's to add. The script sets tabindex="-1" on every control except one, so the toolbar is a single tab stop. Left and Right move focus to the previous and the next control that is rendered and not disabled, and wrap at the ends. Home and End go to the first and the last. On each move the script swaps the tabindex values and calls focus(). Tab leaves the toolbar, and coming back lands on the control that last had focus.
Do not write tabindex="-1" in the markup: without the script those controls could not be reached. The script adds it, and runs again when the 768px change shows or hides controls.
A control that is unavailable carries the disabled attribute, and the reason is in the view, as the count Change 1 of 4 explains a disabled Previous.

The two toggles say whether they are on through aria-pressed, drawn as a fill and a bar. Below 768px the least used group leaves the row and the More menu offers the same actions.

components.name: tooltip
components.title: Tooltip
components.purpose: A line of supplementary text for a control that already has a visible label or an accessible name.
whenToUse: To add a detail to a labelled control: what exactly it will do, or its keyboard shortcut.
To show the name of an icon button to a sighted reader, when the button also carries that name for assistive technology.
whenNotToUse: As the only label of a control. Give the control a visible label or gw-visually-hidden text.
For anything the reader needs in order to act, such as why a button is unavailable or what a field accepts. Write it in the view, for example in the field's description.
For content with a link, a button or more than a sentence. Use a popover.
For an error. Use the field's error or an alert.

variants.name: above
variants.use: The default, with no modifier class. The text sits above the control, from its leading edge.

variants.name: below
variants.use: A control at the top of the screen, such as an action in the app header.

variants.name: end
variants.use: A control at the trailing edge of the view. The text lines up with the control's trailing edge and grows towards the start. It combines with gw-tooltip--below.

accessibility: Wrap the control in a span with the class gw-tooltip, and put the text straight after the control in a span with gw-tooltip__content, role="tooltip" and an id.
The control keeps its own name. Point its aria-describedby at the text, so a screen reader reads the text after the name.
The text holds words only: no link, no button, and nothing the reader cannot find elsewhere.
With that markup alone the tooltip opens on hover and on keyboard focus with no script, and stays open while the pointer is on the text. It closes when the pointer and the focus leave.

Add popover="hint" to the text and interestfor with the text's id to the control. A browser with interest invokers then also opens it on a long press on a touch screen, closes it on Escape, and draws it in the top layer where no container clips it. Other browsers ignore both attributes.

On a touch screen without interest invokers, a tap shows the tooltip only where the browser moves focus to a tapped button. iOS Safari does not. To cover it, the app listens for a long press on the control and calls showPopover({ source: control }) on the text, then hidePopover() on the next press anywhere. The text needs the popover attribute for that.

Without the popover attribute the text is clipped by an ancestor that hides its overflow. Use gw-tooltip--below under the top edge of the screen and gw-tooltip--end at the trailing edge, so the text stays on the screen.

components.name: tree
components.title: Tree
components.purpose: A file tree or an outline whose folders open and close with no script, built on nested details elements.
whenToUse: For the files of a repository, a worktree or a change set, where the reader opens a folder to find a file.
For the outline of a long document or a plan, with sections that hold links to their parts.
Beside the content it navigates, in a sidebar or the list region of a split panel.
whenNotToUse: For items with no hierarchy. Use a list.
For the destinations of the app. Use the sidebar nav.
For one piece of detail that opens in place. Use a disclosure.
For a hierarchy deeper than two levels of folders. Write the rest of the path into the folder's name, such as src/auth/providers, or open the deep folder as a view of its own.
Where items must be selected, dragged or renamed in place with the arrow keys. That is an ARIA tree, which this is not: build it as an app-local component.

variants.name: file tree
variants.use: The default. Each folder's summary holds a folder icon and each file a file icon, both with gw-tree__icon.

variants.name: outline
variants.use: The same markup without the icons, for the sections of a document or a plan.

sizes.name: default
sizes.use: Every row is at least 44px tall. Each level is set in 20px behind a rule.

accessibility: Use a nav with the class gw-tree and an aria-label that says what the tree holds, or a div where the tree does not navigate. Inside it, a ul with gw-tree__list and one li per row.

A folder is a details element with gw-tree__branch. Its summary, with gw-tree__summary, holds an optional icon, the name in a span with gw-tree__name, and optionally a fact in words in a span with gw-tree__meta, such as 3 changed files. After the summary comes a nested ul with gw-tree__list.
A file or an outline entry is an a element with gw-tree__leaf, or a button with type="button" where it selects without navigating. It holds the same icon, name and optional fact.

This is a disclosure tree, not role="tree". The ARIA tree role would oblige the app to script every key, one tab stop, aria-expanded, aria-level, aria-setsize and aria-posinset, and it reads poorly on touch screen readers. Nested details give a screen reader a list with its item count, a button that says collapsed or expanded, and links, with no script at all.

Tab moves through the rows that are shown. Enter or Space on a folder opens or closes it, and Enter follows a file's link. There are no arrow-key bindings, and the browser's find-in-page opens a closed folder that holds a match.
Folders nest at most two levels, the system's limit for disclosures. The checker reports a third as disclosure-depth. Fold a longer path into one folder's name.

Mark the item in view with aria-current on its leaf: "page" for a file that has its own view, "location" for a place in the document, "true" otherwise. It is drawn with a bar and a heavier name as well as a shade. Open the folders that hold it with the open attribute.
Icons are decoration and carry aria-hidden="true". A change is written in words, such as 38 added, 12 removed, never as a colour.
For a folder that is empty, loading or unreadable, put one li with gw-tree__note in its list: a sentence, a spinner with its text, or a sentence with role="alert" and a button that loads again.
To load a folder's rows when it first opens, the app listens for the details element's toggle event. Nothing else needs script.

components.name: undo-toast
components.title: Undo toast
components.purpose: A toast for an action that can be taken back: it says what happened, offers Undo and shows how long Undo stays.
whenToUse: After an action the app carries out at once and can fully reverse, such as archiving a task or removing runs from a board.
In place of a question before a reversible action. Acting and offering Undo is faster than asking first.
whenNotToUse: After an action the app cannot fully reverse, such as deleting a workspace from disk. Ask first with the confirm dialog.
For a message with nothing to take back. Use a toast.
When Undo is the only way back. The reader must also be able to restore the thing elsewhere, such as from an Archived list.

variants.name: words
variants.use: The default. gw-undo-toast__countdown under the message says how many seconds are left.

variants.name: progress
variants.use: A native progress element with gw-undo-toast__progress after the button, as well as the words. Its max is the seconds Undo stays and its value the seconds left.

accessibility: Use the toast markup inside the page's gw-toast__region, with gw-toast, gw-toast--success and gw-undo-toast on the toast element. The message says what happened and to what: Task 41 archived.

Undo is the toast's one action, a button with gw-button gw-button--small gw-toast__action. The toast never takes focus, so also give the reader a way back that does not expire, such as a Restore button in the Archived list.
The app keeps the toast for at least 10 seconds, and pauses its timer while the pointer is over the toast or focus is inside it. When the time runs out the app removes the toast.

Once a second the app writes the seconds left into gw-undo-toast__countdown, and sets the value attribute of the progress element when there is one. Both carry aria-hidden="true", so a screen reader is not interrupted every second. A gw-visually-hidden sentence in the message says the whole time once: You have 10 seconds to undo.

When Undo is pressed, set aria-busy="true" on it, change its label to say what is happening, such as Restoring task, and remove the countdown. Then replace the toast with a plain toast that says the thing is back.
If the undo fails, replace the toast with a gw-toast--danger one that says the thing is still archived and what to do, with Undo again as its action.

components.name: usage-meter
components.title: Usage meter
components.purpose: How much of a limit is used, on a native meter, with the figures and the state written in words.
whenToUse: For use against a known limit: tokens for a run, runs in a month, storage for worktrees.
With the row variant in a cell of a usage table or in a list row, where the row already names what is measured.
whenNotToUse: For the progress of a task towards being done. Use a progress element, or a spinner when the length is not known.
When there is no limit. Write the number as text, or use a stat.
For a number with a comparison and no limit. Use the stat.
For a status. Use a badge.

variants.name: default
variants.use: The label and the state on one line, the bar under them, the figures under the bar.

variants.name: row
variants.use: The bar, the figures and the state on one line, with no label of its own. The meter takes an aria-label that names what the row measures.

accessibility: Use a meter element with the class gw-usage-meter__bar. Set min, max and value from the data, and put the figures as text inside it for a browser that cannot draw it.
Name the meter: aria-labelledby pointing at gw-usage-meter__label, or aria-label in the row variant.
Always write the figures with their unit in gw-usage-meter__figures, such as 18,420 of 50,000 tokens. The bar never stands alone.

The tone comes from the meter's own thresholds, so no class follows the value. Set optimum="0", low to the value where the warning starts and high to the value where the limit is reached or nearly so. The bar is neutral up to low, takes the warning tone between low and high, and the danger tone above high.
Say the same state in words in gw-usage-meter__state, and choose the words by the same thresholds: Within the limit, Near the limit, Over the limit. Colour is never the only signal.
A value above max draws a full bar. Write the real figures, such as 214 of 200 runs, and say what happens next.
With nothing used, keep the meter at 0 and say so. While the figures load, show a spinner in place of the meter. If they cannot be read, show an error message in its place, never an empty bar.
When the state changes while the reader watches, announce it from a role="status" element in the view. The meter is not focusable and needs no script beyond setting its attributes and text.

patterns.name: filter-results
patterns.title: Filter and results
patterns.purpose: A screen that narrows a long list or table: a search field and a few filters above it, the filters in force as removable tags, a count in words, then the results.
whenToUse: For a list or table too long to scan whole, such as every run in a workspace, that the reader narrows by text and by two or three fixed properties.
When the reader needs to see which filters are in force and to remove one without finding its control again.
With a list for results the reader scans and opens, and with a data table when they compare results across columns.
whenNotToUse: For a list short enough to read whole. Show the list with no filters.
For a search over one list with no other filter. Use a search field alone, with its own count line.
For more than three or four filters. Keep the most used in the bar and open the rest in a sheet from a secondary button.
For switching between a few fixed views of one list, such as Open and Closed. Use tabs.
accessibility: In an app the element with gw-filter-results is the main element. The page title is the h1, in a page header, which may hold the view's one primary action. No filter control is primary.

gw-filter-results__bar holds a search field and then each filter as a select in a field. Every control has a visible label, and each select's first option names the unfiltered choice, such as Any status. The results change as a control changes, so the bar has no Apply button.

The filters in force are a ul with an aria-label, holding one removable tag for each, written as the filter's name and value. The search text is one of them. Clear filters is a small quiet button after the list, and it is rendered only while a filter is in force.

The count is a p with gw-filter-results__count and role="status", directly above the results. Keep it in the page from the start and change only its text, after the reader pauses typing, so the new count is announced without moving focus. It says the number, the total and the unit: 3 of 128 runs match.
After a tag is removed, move focus to the next tag's button, or to the search input when none is left.

With no results, the count says 0 and an empty state takes the place of the results. Its title repeats the filters in words, its body names the one filter to loosen and what that would show, and its one button removes that filter. It is never primary.

While results load, the count says what is being searched and a skeleton of rows takes the place of the results, with aria-busy="true" and a gw-visually-hidden line. The filters stay usable. For a wait under about a second, keep the old results and show nothing.
If the results cannot be loaded, show an error state with Retry in their place and keep the filters as the reader set them. Never show the empty state for a failed load.
Tab moves through the search input, its clear button, the filters, each tag's remove button, Clear filters, then the results. The pattern needs no script of its own.

examples.title: Filters in force, a count and the results
examples.reason: Every filter in force is written out as a tag that removes it, so the reader can see why the list is short, and Clear filters undoes them all. The count is in words in a live region directly above the results, and the results are a list, because the runs are alike and are there to be scanned and opened.

patterns.name: master-detail
patterns.title: Master and detail
patterns.purpose: A screen with a list of items and the selected item's detail: side by side from 768px, and on a phone the list alone, with the detail as a view of its own.
whenToUse: When the reader goes through a list item by item and acts on each, such as runs that wait for a decision.
When the detail is short enough to read beside the list: a summary, a few facts and one or two actions.
When the detail is only facts, with no action. Put the catalogue's inspector in the detail's place, using its own layout class.
whenNotToUse: For an item the reader works in for a while, such as a transcript or a diff. Give it a screen of its own and link each row to it.
When the reader compares items with each other. Use a data table.
For a form or a short task that covers the page. Use a sheet or a dialog.
For the app's destinations beside its content. Use the sidebar nav in gw-sidebar-layout.
accessibility: In an app the element with gw-master-detail is the main element. It holds gw-master-detail__list first, then either gw-master-detail__detail or gw-master-detail__placeholder. The list is first in the markup at every width, so Tab reaches the rows before the detail.

The list pane holds the view's h1, in a compact page header, and a list. Each row is a link to the item's own address, so selection works without script and can be bookmarked. Mark the selected row with aria-current="true".

The detail is a section named by its h2, the item's title, through aria-labelledby. Selecting a row does not move focus into it on a wide screen. On a phone the detail is the view, so move focus to its heading.

The phone layout follows from the markup alone. When gw-master-detail__detail is present the list pane is not rendered below 768px, and gw-master-detail__back, a link to the list's address, is the first thing in the detail. From 768px the link is not rendered. With nothing selected, render gw-master-detail__placeholder instead, which is shown only from 768px.

The list keeps its place. When the reader follows the back link, restore the list's scroll position and move focus to the row they came from. From 768px, replace only the detail when the selection changes, and never reorder or refetch the list under the reader.

The view's one primary action is in the detail, written last in a button group. A row has at most one action, a gw-button gw-button--small with secondary emphasis, whose aria-label starts with its visible words and names the row.
An action that discards or stops something carries data-gw-critical and is visible in the detail. It never sits only inside a closed disclosure or a menu.

While the detail loads, keep its heading, set aria-busy="true" on the section and show a skeleton. If it cannot be loaded, show an error state in the detail with Retry. The list stays as it is in both cases.
With no items at all, put an empty state in place of the list and leave both the detail and the placeholder out.

The action that discards work is in sight beside it, and the only row action, Resume, has secondary emphasis. Below 768px the same markup shows the detail as a view of its own, with a link back to the list.

patterns.name: multi-step-form
patterns.title: Multi-step form
patterns.purpose: A longer task split into steps shown one at a time: which step this is in words, the step's fields, Back and one primary action, and a review step before the final action.
whenToUse: For a task with more fields than fit one view comfortably, where later steps depend on earlier answers, such as choosing a repository before writing the task.
When the final action is costly or hard to undo, so the reader should see everything they chose before it runs.
For three to five steps. Each step is its own address, so the browser's back button and a reload both work.
whenNotToUse: For a form that fits one view. Use fields and a button group on one page, and put rarely changed fields in one advanced disclosure.
For one question or one field. Use a dialog.
For settings the reader changes one at a time. Use the settings page.
For sections the reader may fill in any order. Use one page with headings.
accessibility: In an app the element with gw-multi-step-form is the main element. The h1 names the whole task and is the same on every step. Each step is one form, with an h2 that names the step.

gw-multi-step-form__step is a p directly above the h2 that reads Step 2 of 4, in words. When a step loads, move focus to the h2, which takes tabindex="-1", so a screen reader reads the step's name, and put the step in the document title.
To show the named steps above the form, with the completed and current ones marked, use the stepper component. Keep the step line in words as well.

Every step ends with a button group. The secondary action comes first: Back, a link to the previous step that keeps what was typed, or Cancel on the first step. The primary action comes last: Continue on every step but the last.

The last step is the review. It shows every answer in a key-value list, in the order the steps asked for them, then one sentence on what the final action does. Its primary button is a specific verb and what it acts on, such as Start task, never Submit or Finish.

Validate a step when it is sent. Keep the reader on the step, add an alert with role="alert" above the fields whose title counts the fields to fix and whose body names them, mark each field with aria-invalid="true" and its own error message, and move focus to the first invalid field.
A field's error says how to fix the value. Remove the error and aria-invalid when the value is fixed, and remove the alert when none is left.
While a step is sent, set aria-busy="true" on the primary button and change its label to say what is happening, such as Starting task.
Nothing the reader must fill in sits inside a closed disclosure. A step may hold one advanced disclosure for optional fields that have defaults.
Tab moves through the fields in order, then Back, then the primary action. Enter in a text input sends the step. The pattern needs no script of its own.

patterns.name: not-found
patterns.title: Not found
patterns.purpose: The screen for a missing page or a missing item: what was not found in plain words, why that might be, one primary way forward and a quiet second link.
whenToUse: When an address matches no screen in the app.
When the screen exists and the item it should show does not, such as a deleted run, or one in a repository the reader cannot see.
Inside the app's usual header, so the reader still has the app's own ways out.
whenNotToUse: When the item may exist and loading it failed. Use an error state with Retry, so the reader is not told something is gone when it may not be.
When a list or a search has no results. Use an empty state in place of the results, as the filter and results pattern does.
When the reader is signed out. Send them to the sign-in screen and bring them back afterwards.
For a section of a view that has nothing in it. Use an empty state in that section.
accessibility: In an app the element with gw-not-found is the main element, under the app header. It holds an empty state and then one quiet link.

The empty state's title is the page's h1. It says what was not found, naming the address or the item: Run 4182 was not found. A status code is not a title. Put the same words in the document title, and send the 404 status with the page.
The body is one or two sentences giving the likely reasons, and what the reader can do when the reason is access. It does not blame the reader and makes no joke.

The one action in the empty state is a link with the primary button classes, to a screen that exists and that most readers want next, such as the list the item belonged to. It names where it goes. Never use Go back, which may return to the broken link.
The second way forward is a gw-link gw-link--quiet after the empty state, such as a search with the missing name already filled in.
Do not tell a reader without access whether the item exists. Use the same words for a deleted item and for one they may not see.
There is no illustration and no icon. When the page loads, focus starts at the top of the document as usual, and Tab reaches the header, the primary link, then the quiet link.

examples.reason: The title says what was not found, with the address the reader asked for. The sentence gives the two likely reasons in plain words. One primary link goes to the screen most readers want next, and a quiet link offers the other way to find something. There is no picture, no code number as a headline and no joke.

patterns.name: settings-page
patterns.title: Settings page
patterns.purpose: A screen of settings shown defaults first: the few settings most people change, one advanced disclosure holding the rest, and a marked danger area for actions that destroy something.
whenToUse: For the settings of one thing, such as a repository, a runner or an account, when a few of them are changed often and the rest rarely.
Save-on-change: every control saves the moment it changes. Use switches and selects, say so in the page description, and give the page no primary action.
Explicit save: the settings take effect together. Make the page a form with checkboxes in place of switches, and one primary button that names what it saves.
whenNotToUse: For one or two settings that belong to a view. Put a switch or a select in that view.
For a task with an order to it, such as connecting a repository. Use the multi-step form.
For settings in several unrelated groups, each long enough to scroll. Give each group a screen of its own, linked from the sidebar nav, and use this pattern on each.
For facts the reader cannot change. Use a key-value list.

variants.name: save on change
variants.use: Each control saves as it changes. The page description says so, a failed save is reported on the control that failed, and there is no primary button.

variants.name: explicit save
variants.use: The page is one form. Its primary button, written last in a button group after a secondary Discard changes, is the only primary action, and a status line above it says what is not saved yet.

accessibility: In an app the element with gw-settings-page is the main element. The examples use a div because a gallery page holds several of them.
The page title is the h1, in a page header. Each group of settings starts with an h2, and the danger area is a card whose title is an h2 that says Danger area and what it belongs to.

Every setting keeps the markup of its own component: a switch for a setting saved at once, a checkbox inside a form, a select or a text input in a field. Each has a visible label, and a default is already chosen.
For a setting written as one row, with its label and description at the start and its control at the far end, use the settings row component.

There is exactly one details element with data-gw-advanced in the view. Its summary reads Advanced settings and counts what is inside in a gw-disclosure__meta span. It starts closed, and nothing the reader must set before the page works goes inside it.

Every action in the danger area carries data-gw-critical and gw-button--danger, is visible without opening anything, and sits beside a sentence that says what is lost. Ask before it runs with a confirm dialog.
Save-on-change: when a save fails, set the control back and add its component's error element with role="alert", saying which state the setting is in and what to do.

Explicit save: the line that says what is unsaved has role="status". While the form is sent, set aria-busy="true" on the primary button and change its label to Saving settings. Report a failed save in an alert above the button group.

While the settings load, a skeleton stands in for the groups, with aria-busy="true" and a gw-visually-hidden line that says what is loading. If they cannot be loaded, show an error state in its place.
Tab moves through the settings in reading order, then the advanced summary, then the danger area. The pattern needs no script of its own.

Every change is saved at once, so the page needs no primary action, and the two actions that destroy something stay in sight in a marked area of their own.

patterns.name: sign-in
patterns.title: Sign in
patterns.purpose: The sign-in screen: the product's name, one sentence, the fields, one primary action and a quiet link for trouble signing in, in a reading-width column at the leading edge.
whenToUse: For the screen a signed-out reader meets before anything else in the app.
For any other single focused task that stands outside the app's navigation, such as setting a new password or accepting an invitation. Keep the same shape: a name, a sentence, the fields, one action.
whenNotToUse: To ask for the password again inside the app, before a sensitive action. Use a dialog.
To describe or promote the product. This screen has no hero, no feature list and no picture. That belongs on the product's site.
For creating an account in several steps. Use the multi-step form.
With the app header or the navigation around it. A signed-out reader has nowhere to go, so the screen shows neither.
accessibility: In an app the element with gw-sign-in is the main element, and it is the only landmark on the page. The column starts at the leading edge of the page and is never centred.
gw-sign-in__product is a p holding the product's name. The h1 after it reads Sign in, and one sentence under it says which account to use. There is no other copy.

The fields are in one form. The email input has type="email" and autocomplete="username", and the password input has type="password" and autocomplete="current-password", so a password manager can fill both. Neither uses a placeholder as its label.
Sign in is the form's submit button and the screen's one primary action. The link for trouble signing in is a quiet link after the form, and it names what it does.

When the sign-in is refused, keep the email, clear the password, and add an alert with role="alert" as the first thing in the form. Its title says what happened and its body says what to do. Link it from both inputs with aria-describedby, and move focus to the password input. Do not say which field was wrong.
While the form is sent, set aria-busy="true" on the button, change its label to Signing in, make the inputs read-only and ignore further presses.
Tab moves through Email, Password, Sign in, then the help link. Enter in either input sends the form. The pattern needs no script of its own.
